scope: Explicitly dated, recoverable new concrete record findings and supported factual corrections. Dates and explicit date ranges are research retrieval, supplied-record review or original-reading dates stated in the maintained evidence, not the dates of historical events or file modification. Undated historical conclusions, pure confirmations, speculative parent rankings, negative searches and routine profile/build activity are excluded. This is a recoverable dated history, not an exhaustive account of all past research.

findings.finding: The Larne session minutes naming John Glasgow, sen., Robert Glasgow and James Glasgow belong to 1700 and 1701, not 1699 and 1700. John and Robert were stipend bondsmen for Kilwaughter and the South Side on 17 May 1700; James was made overseer for Kilwaughter probably on Thursday 29 May 1701.
findings.qualification: Porter prints the minutes under 1699 and 1700 from a manuscript copy of the session record. He corrects the stipend run to 1700 himself and the weekdays confirm it; the 1701 date for James is an inference from the weekdays. The minutes state no relationship between the three men. No live WikiTree change.

sources.title: Porter, Congregational Memoirs: Larne and Kilwaughter, The Christian Unitarian 2 (1863), pp. 410-414
The same, The Christian Unitarian 3 (1864), pp. 16-19

findings.finding: The Robert Glasgow marked “turned out” on the Larne session list of 1721-1769 and the Robert Glasgow of the discipline minute of 17 May 1747 are one man, probably Robert Glasgow of Kilwaughter (Glasgow-1143) and not the Robert of 1700-01.
findings.qualification: Porter’s footnote ties the list note to the 1747 minute. The identification rests on age (the older Robert would have been in his late sixties or more) and Kilwaughter residence; no record states it, and a third Robert cannot be excluded. No live WikiTree change.

findings.finding: William Agnew’s lease of Ballykeel to Robert Glasgow is dated 13 February 1738 Old Style (1739 by modern reckoning) and was registered on 22 May 1742. Its three lives are Robert, “Jas Glasgow Junr” and Rachel “otherwise Wilson Wife to the sd Robt Glasgow”; it names no second James and gives Robert no residence.
findings.qualification: Read on the saved register images of memorial 74015 by two readers. “Junior” points to an older namesake and states no relationship. No live WikiTree change.

findings.finding: Robert Glasgow of Kilwaughter was alive on 20 December 1764, when he leased half of Ballykeel to Hugh Shannon, and probably in April 1772. “About 1772” is a last sighting, not a death estimate, and “about 1710” would make him a groom of 19; about 1708 or earlier fits the records.
findings.qualification: No record gives his age or his death. The 1772 declaration’s date and Kilwaughter heading are known only second-hand. The WikiTree dates are queued for review, not changed.

findings.finding: Rachel Wilson’s birth “about 1680” has no source and would make her 51, 53 and 58 at the baptisms of her children in 1731, 1733 and 1738. The records allow about 1690 to 1712.
findings.qualification: An estimate: it assumes a bride of at least about 17 in November 1729 and a mother of no more than about 48 in November 1738. The marriage and baptisms are known from a derivative register chronology. The WikiTree date is queued for review, not changed.

findings.finding: Porter prints one pall entry for William Glasgow: in 1734 the new pall “was to be lodged with William Glasgow Major”. The mortcloth receipts of 1739/40, 1741 and 1743 are not in Porter; they come from a derivative account of the session book.
findings.qualification: “Major” may mean “the elder” (possible only). The later receipts stay unverified until PRONI MIC/1B/6 is read. No live WikiTree change.

findings.finding: The ruling elder James Glasgow of the General Synod rolls is printed beside William Taylor of Drumaul in 1698 and 1703 and beside James Scott of Duneane in 1705; Larne’s own elder in 1703 was James Caldwell. He is probably not James Glasgow of Kilwaughter.
findings.qualification: The rolls print no congregation for an elder. That the 1705 elder is the man of 1698 and 1703 is possible, not established. No Glasgow is printed as Larne’s elder in any roll from 1694 to 1720, which shows only who represented Larne at Synod. No live WikiTree change.

findings.finding: The informant at Alexander Glasgow’s death at Gortahar on 16 May 1888 reads Mary Glasgow, daughter, not Nancy. The forename matches the registrar’s “Mary” in three nearby entries and differs from his “Nancy” in a fourth.
findings.qualification: Read from the registrar’s quarterly copy; the local register original has not been viewed. Alexander’s daughter Mary was Mrs Elder by 1888, so the surname Glasgow is unexplained: a maiden-name entry, his wife Mary with the relationship mis-entered, or Mary Ellen Glasgow (born 1867) remain possible. All three belong to the Lisnagaver family. No live WikiTree change.

findings.finding: Four original-checked Belfast News-Letter passages from 1840 name Rev. Adam Glasgow: as officiant at a James and Margaret Small marriage, as opening a Townsend-street Presbyterian soirée, among speakers at the Belfast Town Mission annual meeting, and among two Synod ministers accepted for India mission service with James Carr. The Synod report says Kathiawar or Guzerat was selected and gives a planned 4 August departure overland to Bombay.
findings.qualification: The notices give no middle name or unique identifier; the ministerial context is compatible with, but does not uniquely identify, Glasgow-1781. “Wednesday evening last” for the Town Mission meeting is retained as printed. The August journey is planned, not proof of departure. The separate Synod passage names James Carr, not James Glasgow, and establishes no kinship. The 1842 Nancy marriage notice is not included here because the same fact was already documented; it is added only as primary-source corroboration.

findings.finding: Original-checked Belfast News-Letter passages name James Glasgow as a Belfast College essay award recipient in 1829; Rev. James Glasgow of Castledawson at a Bellaghy ordination in 1836 and among missionaries set apart for India in 1840; a source of a letter reported in 1841; the signer of a Rajkote letter dated 14 August 1841; and the first Moderator of the first Indian Presbytery in 1842.
findings.qualification: The 1829 student is only a possible match to Glasgow-1780. The Castledawson and missionary passages are probable matches within the established career sequence, but these notices do not give James’s middle name. The 1836 ordination date (15 March) is inferred from “15th ult.”; the issue date is 5 April. The 1841 May report gives no letter date; the October letter is dated 14 August. The separate Adam Glasgow passages on the 1840 and 1842 issues do not establish kinship. “Brother missionary” describes colleague Alexander Kerr, not a biological brother. No family certainty changes.

findings.finding: James Glasgow is named in the Greenock arrival list headed “Greenock, August 12”: “The Prosperity of Irvine, James Glasgow, from Northcopen.” The item was published in The Caledonian Mercury on 18 August 1740, page 3.

HOLD — one documentary occurrence, four compatible Irvine candidates. The original confirms the surname reading; it does not select a profile. margaret-glasgow.assessment: Betham’s manuscript pedigree of Archibald Glasgow, Rathmalton clerk, whose will was dated April 1673, expressly names Margaret as his only daughter, married to an unnamed Cairns, with son Thomas Cairns. This proves the documentary father–daughter pair. Glasgow-3186, wife of George Lyell in South Leith in 1633, remains a candidate because a later Cairns marriage is possible, but no marriage or household bridge is proved. The Scottish Archibald profile identity remains qualified; no profile father upgrade follows. Glasgow-1523’s cited 1638 baptism names father William Glasgow, a concrete father conflict; its guessed 1642 death is not evidence.

findings.finding: Daniel Glasco, Norfolk planter, conveyed 100 acres to Richard Linton with the consent of Mary, explicitly his wife. The court endorsement says Daniel personally acknowledged the deed on 3 September 1729, establishing survival to that date.
findings.qualification: Inspected original deed endorsement. No father is stated; profile identification and the earlier William title recital remain qualified. Registration alone is not used as a life boundary.

sources.title: Princess Anne County, Deeds and Wills Book4 Part1 (1724–1735), manuscript p.207, DGS7645780

daniel-glasco.assessment: Daniel Glasco/Glascow, Norfolk planter, and his wife Mary conveyed 100 acres from Henry Slade’s 330-acre patent to Richard Linton. The upper endorsement expressly says Daniel came into court and acknowledged the act on 3 September 1729, proving him alive then. Daneill Glasco and Richard Linton also witnessed Richard Johnson’s will dated 26 February 1729/30; McIntosh’s abstract is printed page 122. Glasgow-3322, Mary Gamon’s husband in 1693, remains compatible, but the two estates have no proved continuous title chain.

mary.assessment: Mary is expressly Daniel Glasco’s wife in the 1729 deed. Gammon-934 remains compatible with the 1693 John Gamon will’s daughter Mary, wife of Daniel Glasco. Her guessed 1699 death and inconsistent imported spouse field are unsupported and do not exclude her. The 1693 record proves that earlier Mary’s father, but no record yet proves that the 1729 wife is the same woman. Keep the candidate and the lifetime identity qualification together.

richard-linton.assessment: Richard Linton purchased the 1729 land and witnessed Richard Johnson’s will dated 26 February 1729/30 with Daneill Glasco. Linton-898 remains compatible: its estimated 1680 birth, missing death and sparse Virginia family context supply no concrete conflict. Linton-931 also remains a weaker compatible candidate because its 1722 birth is GEDCOM-derived. Linton-494 has cited Lancaster death/probate in 1665, a concrete conflict with the 1729 transaction. Keep the candidate; cite McIntosh’s printed page 122 and do not infer survival to probate.

mary-glasgon-thomson.assessment: The 1860 marriage index names the bride’s mother Mary Glasgon Thomson. Glasgow-4093, Nancy’s daughter Mary Thompson in the 1892 New York probate, remains a candidate without an Irish–Scottish household bridge. Glasgow-1351, Glasgow-1353, Glasgow-1453 and Glasgow-1531 also remain candidates; their Scottish baptismal families have no proved Robert Thomson marriage connection. Do not transfer a Tannybrake widow’s age or identify Nancy as this mother. The original marriage image requires a FamilySearch center or affiliate library and was not inspected.

mary-thomson.assessment: Mary Thomson, age 37, married William Sneddon on 9 November 1860; the fresh index names her parents Robert Thomson and Mary Glasgon Thomson. Thomson-3009 remains a disputed candidate because its estimated 1826 birth and James/Helen GEDCOM parents are unsupported. Thomson-13010 has record-based Andrew Thomson/Elizabeth Waddell parents and a distinct Abercrombie household, a concrete conflict with the indexed bride. Index parentage is not an existing-profile father upgrade, and the restricted original remains uninspected.

william-sneddon.assessment: The fresh 1860 index identifies William Sneddon, age 45, widower and collier, with parents Robert Sneddon and Mary Gray Sneddon. Sneddon-710 remains a candidate: its Pencaitland coal-mining household and wife Mary Wilson allow a later widowed marriage. However, age 30 in 1841 normally means 30–34, implying birth about 1806–1811 rather than the 1860 estimate of 1815. This is a material discrepancy. No record joins the indexed parents to Sneddon-710. Obtain the 1851/1861 census, first wife’s death and accessible original; do not attach Sneddon-92, whose recorded wife was Mary Snaddon, daughter of Richard Snaddon and Mary Hoggan.

archibald-herbertsoun.assessment: The 18 January 1581/82 Bridgegait boundary names Archibald Herbertsoun, fisher. findings.finding: A deed dated 12 May 1772 names Wm Glasgow of Larne as a witness; it was registered on 9 November 1784.
findings.qualification: Original manuscript inspected. No age, occupation or relative distinguishes the older and younger William; registration does not establish survival to 1784.

findings.finding: Memorial 173104 records James Glasgow, ropemaker, assigning the ropewalk and workhouse to John Hill on 28 March 1768; a second James Glasgow witnesses as tanner.
findings.qualification: Original occupation reading checked. This distinguishes the principal from his same-name witness, but does not establish the tanner’s family identity.

findings.finding: An 1874 indenture traces James Glasgow’s 2 October 1779 Newtown of Larne lease to a 25 February 1832 renewal to Anne and Jane Glasgow.
findings.qualification: Original recital inspected. It establishes title succession, not stated descent; James and both women’s identities remain unresolved.

james-glasgow.assessment: The live biographies identify two distinct adult Larne men: James Glasgow-1509, ropemaker (1737–1802), and James Glasgow-3991, probable tanner (about 1748–1812). Both survived until the 1779 lease. The separate 1768 messuage names a ropemaker party and a farmer witness, whose roles require separate comparison. Glasgow-1509 is the leading compatible party. No source names the farmer witness's relatives or identifies the 1779 lessee. The 1832 renewal does not establish Anne or Jane as James’s daughters. Keep the 1768 ropemaker party, farmer witness and 1779 lessee roles separate. Jane, wife of Glasgow-3991, died in 1820 and cannot be the 1832 lessee.

anne-glasgow.assessment: Ann Glasgow-3992, born about 1768, died on 25 May 1832 at Larne and was alive on the 25 February 1832 renewal date. Her armorial inscription names father James and mother Jane, fitting the local generation, but does not identify this lease. Ann and Anne are compatible name forms. The 1832 renewal does not establish Anne or Jane as James’s daughters. Keep the 1768 ropemaker party, farmer witness and 1779 lessee roles separate. Jane, wife of Glasgow-3991, died in 1820 and cannot be the 1832 lessee.

jane-glasgow.assessment: Jane Glasgow-4013 is the strongest locality candidate: her live biography describes Larne probate entries in 1844–1846 and birth before 1826, rather than an actual 1826 birth. Jane Glasgow-3929, born 5 October 1802 and later wife of John Gray, is also chronologically compatible. A different husband and missing lease connection do not exclude her. The 1832 renewal does not establish Anne or Jane as James’s daughters. Keep the 1768 ropemaker party, farmer witness and 1779 lessee roles separate. Jane, wife of Glasgow-3991, died in 1820 and cannot be the 1832 lessee.

findings.finding: The separate memorial 173108 records James Glasgow, ropemaker, assigning a messuage to John Hill on 28 March 1768; its witnessing James Glasgow is described as farmer.
findings.qualification: Original occupation checked. The same-day ropewalk and messuage assignments are different instruments. Whether the farmer and tanner witnesses are one man is unresolved.

findings.finding: The 1912 Belfast and Ulster Directory lists Nancy McCaughern as a publican among the inhabitants of Rasharkin. It is a useful later record for separating McCaughern women in the locality, but it must not be conflated with Nancy Glasgow, with the Nancy McCaughern named on the James McCaughern memorial, or with any other McCaughern profile without an address, age or family record.
findings.qualification: Inspected named transcription or derivative source; original record uninspected and family identity not established.

nancy-mccaughern.assessment: McCarnagh-4 represents Agnes, born about 1837 at Gortereghy, daughter of John McCarnagh and Mary Gormley in 1851. Agnes/Nancy and McCarnagh/McCaughern are compatible forms; an age of about 75 in 1912 is possible. No cited biography supplies a death or contradictory publican household. This is a weak compatible candidate, not proof of occupational identity.

findings.finding: The 1912 Belfast and Ulster Directory lists Thomas Ross as a mill owner at Gortreighy in the neighbourhood inhabitants section for Rasharkin. It adds a named economic and geographic associate in the townland where the Glasgow family lived in the earlier baptism period, but it does not establish any relationship to Alexander Glasgow or the McCaughan/Elder families.
findings.qualification: Inspected named transcription or derivative source; original record uninspected and family identity not established.

thomas-ross.assessment: The original 1901 Gortereghy return describes Thomas Ross, 34, as farmer and flax miller, with Scotland-born wife Mary Jane and children. This strongly supports the 1912 mill-owner occurrence. The 1911 household reports 24 years of marriage. Ross-13124 remains compatible, with differing reported census ages. Ross-29596 has severe chronology tension if his cited 1874 birth is correct: he would be about 12 at marriage and 11 when Jeannie was born. The birth image returned HTTP 403, so this remains a conditional conflict rather than a fresh original-based exclusion. Ross-25888 has a separate Gransha/Ann Jane family; Ross-29600 is Robert T Ross, who died in 1909.

findings.finding: The published headstone transcription for Rasharkin Second Presbyterian Church records a memorial erected by Alexander Elder of Gortrickey to his father Robert Elder, his mother Jane, and his sisters and brothers. It also records Alexander Elder's death on 5 January 1943.
findings.qualification: This is a new direct memorial transcription for the catalogue's parentage study, not a Glasgow record and not proof that the Elder family was related to Alexander Glasgow. Its value is locality context: Gortrickey/Gortereghy is the townland where the Glasgow family appears in the 1837–1838 Rasharkin Presbyterian baptism entries. The memorial supplies a named Elder household for future comparison with the later Robert Elder who occupied Alexander Glasgow's former Lisnagaver lot; identity between those Elder references remains unproved.

people.name: Alexander Elder
people.role: Sourced record subject; identity remains qualified

robert-elder-father.assessment: Elder-7144 remains compatible for the living 1901 father of Alex/Robert/Eliza/Margaretta; its 1827 birth is tree-derived and differs from reported age 65, so retain uncertainty. Elder-7251 represents Mary Glasgow’s separate Gortahar family: she is a widow there in 1901 while the Gortereghy Robert is alive. Do not exclude Elder-7251 globally from Sarah’s 1893 father clause merely because a father can be deceased at marriage. Sarah and Isaac’s father occurrences remain unproved bridges to the 1901 family. The original 1881 Jane birth proves Robert/Jane Calderwood as a parental couple, not the mother identity of all later siblings.

alexander-elder.assessment: The original 1901 Alex is explicitly Robert’s son; the 1911 return names brother Robert and sister Margaret. Together with the 1908 Alexander/Mary Anderson marriage extract, these support one sibling family. Retain the actual age differences. Use the same qualified Elder-7144 father hypothesis for Alexander and proved siblings; mother Jane on the memorial is separately evidenced, while Jane Calderwood remains a comparison. No matching Alexander profile was established in full same-name and father-filtered searches.

findings.finding: The original civil birth return records Mary Ellen, a female child born at Lisnagaver on 14 February 1867. The mother is Mary Glasgow; no father is entered.
findings.qualification: Original register or Form A inspected on 30 September 2026; source-specific image and entry references supplied. Profile identities and cross-record continuity remain qualified where stated.

mary-ellen.assessment: The same-record identification is strong. Glasgow-4269 cites the GRONI index for Mary Glasgow, Ballymoney, February 1867, reference U/1867/31/1005/2/214. The inspected original Ballymoney/Dirraw return, printed page 6 and PDF page 1, entry 214, records Mary Ellen at Lisnagaver, mother Mary Glasgow and informant Ann Glasgow. No competing local February 1867 child was found. The original reads fourteenth February, while the index and profile give 17 February. This is a date conflict within the identified registration, not grounds to duplicate the child.

mary-glasgow.assessment: The 1867 mother Mary Glasgow and Mary Glasgow-3167, born about 1843 and a 28-year-old Lisnagaver spinster in the original marriage of 14 June 1871, share name, locality and compatible age. An earlier child of an unmarried mother fits the later spinster description. The birth names no father and does not itself establish which Mary she was.

ann-glasgow.assessment: The original 1867 informant Ann Glasgow of Lisnagaver is compatible with Ann Glasgow-438, Alexander and Mary's daughter aged four in 1851 and later a Lisnagaver spinster at her 1876 marriage. Her age of about 20 in 1867 and repeated address support the candidate. The birth does not call her the mother's sister.

findings.finding: The 1912 Belfast and Ulster Directory lists Peter McCaughern as a grocer and farmer among the inhabitants of Rasharkin. It may be relevant to the later Rasharkin McCaughern probate network, but the directory gives no age, address or family relationship, so this Peter must not be merged with the Peter McCaughern of the 1916 Dreen probate cluster without further evidence.
findings.qualification: Inspected named transcription or derivative source; original record uninspected and family identity not established.

peter-mccaughern.assessment: The original 1911 Dreen return names Peter McCaughern, 48, single Roman Catholic farmer, and his sister Agnes, 55. This is a concrete family comparison for the 1912 grocer/farmer and later Dreen probates. Directory-to-census continuity remains probable; the probate original was not inspected. Searches for McCaughern, McCaughan, McCarnagh and McCahern identified no supported profile. No father is evidenced.

findings.finding: The reproduced Third Portglenone Presbyterian marriage list records Robert Elder, full-age bachelor labourer of Ballymoney, marrying Jane Adams McCaughey, full-age spinster of Garvaghey, on 13 July 1887. Robert's father is recorded as James Elder, labourer; Jane's father as William McCaughey, labourer.
findings.qualification: The witnesses were Archie McCaughey and Lizzie Connaghy. It is useful chiefly as a confirmed namesake-separation record: this Robert should not be merged with Robert Elder, Mary's 1871 husband, whose father was recorded as Nathaniel Elder and whose occupation was farmer. The source is a secondary transcription and the original register remains to be inspected.

robert-elder.assessment: Robert Elder-3949, son of James Elder and Mary Jane McAughin, was born on 21 September 1858 in the local Gortereghy/Ballymoney family. His live biography gives no conflicting spouse or later chronology. He is compatible with the full-age Ballymoney labourer in 1887 whose father James was a labourer; an occupational change does not exclude him. Identification remains unproved without an original marital-status and address chain. James Elder-3946 is a possible father identity for the marriage clause, but that identity and mother Mary Jane are not proved by the 1887 marriage alone.

jane-adams-mccaughey.assessment: No compatible separate Jane Adams McCaughey profile was identified in the completed Jane McCaughey/McCaughe searches. The similarly aged McCaughey-347 represents a Montreal woman whose profile lacks the named William/Garvaghey connection. It remains a name-only lead, not a proved exclusion.

william-mccaughey.assessment: No supported William McCaughey profile was identified for the father named in Jane Adams's 1887 marriage. Completed William McCaughey/McCaughe searches include William McCaughey-350, born in 1860 and son of James, and an unplaced eighteenth-century William McCaughey-204. Neither has a sourced match to a Garvaghey daughter Jane Adams. Unplaced profiles are not excluded merely for absent fields.

mary-kilpatrick.assessment: Kilpatrick-3023 represents Mary, born about 1820 and died in 1870, associated with Larne/Antrim. findings.finding: The original 1911 Gortahar census reports Samuel Glasgow, aged two; his 4 July 1908 civil birth names him Samuel Elder, son of unmarried Jane Elder, with no father recorded.

findings.finding: Mary Glasgow, widow, housewife, aged 89, died at Gortahar on 17 February 1892; daughter Mary Elder was present. The formerly maintained 27 February date was a transcription error. Identification with Mary McCaughan is strongly supported through the 1871 Elder–Glasgow marriage and Lisnagaver family evidence.
findings.qualification: Original register image and enlarged entry independently checked. Identification with Mary McCaughan is strongly supported by the daughter and family evidence; the death return does not name her maiden surname.

findings.finding: Jane Matilda Elder was born at Gortahar to farmer Robert Elder and Mary Elder, whose maiden surname is entered as Glass; Robert, her father, informed the birth. Exact parents, place and middle initial identify the later Jane M. Elder.
findings.qualification: Original civil birth inspected. The mother’s maiden surname is recorded as Glass. Exact parents, place and middle initial support identification with the later Jane M. Elder; census ages conflict.

david-mathy.assessment: David Mathy and Mergaret Androsoune, expressly his spouse, bought a barn at Powdrait, Glasgow, on 3 February 1550/51. David Mathy and Robert Glesgw were expressly fellow burgesses witnessing a sasine on 10 May 1554; David also witnessed an act on 4 July 1554. The name and city make the purchaser and witness probably the same man, but the later acts do not repeat the spouse. No kinship with Robert is stated. David Matthew-330 is a weak compatible variant candidate: its only 1701 death assertion is GEDCOM-derived, so it cannot be excluded. The complete sourced draft remains on HOLD against that candidate, with purchaser/witness identity qualified.

david-mathy.assessment: David Mathy and Mergaret Androsoune, expressly his spouse, bought a barn at Powdrait, Glasgow, on 3 February 1550/51. David Mathy and Robert Glesgw were expressly fellow burgesses witnessing a sasine on 10 May 1554; David also witnessed an act on 4 July 1554. The name and city make the purchaser and witness probably the same man, but the later acts do not repeat the spouse. No kinship with Robert is stated. David Matthew-330 is a weak compatible variant candidate: its only 1701 death assertion is GEDCOM-derived, so it cannot be excluded. The complete sourced draft remains on HOLD against that candidate, with purchaser/witness identity qualified.

margaret-androsoune.assessment: Mergaret Androsoune is expressly David Mathy’s spouse in the 3 February 1550/51 Glasgow barn purchase. No age, birthplace, parents, children or death is stated. Anderson-3241 is a sparse compatible candidate with unknown dates, Scotland locality and an unsupported John Kelman spouse; no record proves identity or a conflict. The spouse clause is certain for the documentary couple, while her existing-profile identity remains unresolved.

findings.finding: The official description of Stirling charter B66/25/43, dated 8 August 1475, groups John Glesgw among burgess witnesses. It supplies civic status and a third source-described occurrence alongside the known April 1475 and March 1479/80 acts.
findings.qualification: Archive description inspected; original charter not seen. The three Stirling occurrences are a high-confidence working identity. Glasgow-1095 remains a compatible imported-profile candidate, with Saltmarket as its maintained research destination; no identity or father relationship is newly proved. One man across Glasgow 1447–1455 and Stirling 1475–1480 remains viable, as do close-family alternatives.
